newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE - India oil subsidy brings tears to the eyes.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - India oil subsidy brings tears to the eyes.

text.p: India's complex subsidy system for petroleum products literally brings tears to the eyes and an unpleasant tickle in the throat -- thanks to the noxious traffic fumes polluting towns and cities.

Scooters, three-wheeler autorickshaws and beaten-up cars dodge down busy roads, their exhaust pipes spewing choking gases from an illegal kerosene-petrol mix, or a kerosene-diesel brew that is more harmful to engines than lungs.
The adulterated fuels are the illegal offspring of India's cross-subsidy scheme.
Under the "administered pricing mechanism", petrol and other premium products are priced artificially high in order to offset heavily subsidised fuels used by the country's poor.
Oil industry executives and analysts say they hope the government does not widen the differential between petrol and the middle distillates.
A decision on oil prices is expected later this month, and despite abuse of the system, expectations are that any increase in kerosene prices will lag behind the others.
"If this happens, as seems probable, we will see a larger quantity of kerosene going into adulteration," R.K. Pachouri, director of the independent Tata Energy Research, told Reuters.
Junior Petroleum Minister T.R. Balu is set to meet Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral on Thursday to discuss prices.
And the topic is likely to head the agenda when the United Front 15-member coalition's policy-vetting steering committee meets on May 25.
Currently, petrol in India costs up to 24 rupees (67 U.S. cents) a litre, and is overpriced by roughly 20 percent.
Diesel is sold at seven rupees a litre, and carries a two rupee subsidy. The subsidy on kerosene, which sells at two rupees a litre, is five rupees.
Filling station owners make an easy profit mixing the products and undercutting legal prices or selling at regular prices to unwitting motorists.
Petrol consumption, at around five million tonnes, accounts for just seven percent of the total petroleum product consumption of some 78 million tonnes a year.
Diesel consumption is more than 35 million tonnes annually, used mainly in agriculture, cars and some power stations.
Kerosene is the basic cooking and lighting fuel for about 300 million poor Indians, who make up families in the lower middle-class bracket and below.
The very poor make do with wood, and the government hopes low kerosene prices will help retard deforestation.

But of the 10 million tonnes of kerosene consumed annually, less than 50 percent ends up in the right hands, according to some analysts, although the Petroleum Ministry said it is more like 20-25 percent.
"The pity of this subsidy is that the target population does not get the benefit, only a small fraction of them get it, the bulk goes to the wrong people," Pachouri said.
Somewhere along the distribution system the rest is siphoned off into the nationwide filling-pump scam.

Devi Dayal, additional secretary in the marketing section of the Petroleum Ministry, said state governments' will have to ensure buyers hold genuine ration cards entitling them to subsidised prices to plug leaks in the distribution system.
Ironically, the petrol profiteers' greatest defenders are India's leftist parties, who are adamantly opposed to any reduction in the kerosene subsidy that would hurt their voters.
